content: The 2013 guidelines for HIV testing, counseling, antiretroviral therapy (ART), and service delivery provide specific recommendations for various populations and settings. 1. HIV Testing and Counseling in Community Settings: In areas with generalized HIV epidemics, community-based HIV testing and counseling (CBTC) linked to prevention, care, and treatment services is recommended. This is in addition to provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC). This recommendation is strong, though based on low-quality evidence. For key populations in all epidemic settings, CBTC with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services is also recommended alongside PITC. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 2. HIV Testing and Counseling for Adolescents: Adolescents from key populations in all settings (generalized, low, and concentrated epidemics) should have access to HIV testing and counseling linked to prevention, treatment, and care. This is a strong recommendation, though based on very low-quality evidence. In generalized epidemics, HIV testing and counseling linked to prevention, treatment, and care is recommended for all adolescents. This is a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. In low and concentrated epidemics, it is suggested that HIV testing and counseling linked to prevention, treatment, and care be accessible to all adolescents. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. Adolescents should be counseled on the potential benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV status. They should be empowered and supported to decide if, when, how, and to whom to disclose. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 3. When to Start ART in People Living with HIV: Adults and Adolescents: ART should be initiated in all individuals with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) or with a CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. ART should also be initiated in individuals with a CD4 count between 350 and 500 cells/mm³, regardless of WHO clinical stage. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. ART should be started in all individuals with HIV, regardless of CD4 count or clinical stage, in the following situations: Those with active tuberculosis (TB) disease (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Those co-infected with HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV) with evidence of severe chronic liver disease (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). HIV-positive partners in serodiscordant couples to reduce HIV transmission to the uninfected partner (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). 4. When to Start ART in Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women: All pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV should initiate triple antiretroviral therapy (ART) and maintain it at least for the duration of the risk of mother-to-child transmission. Women meeting treatment eligibility criteria should continue lifelong ART. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. For programmatic and operational reasons, especially in generalized epidemics, all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV should initiate lifelong ART. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. In some countries, for women not eligible for ART for their own health, stopping the ART regimen after the period of mother-to-child transmission risk has ceased can be considered. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 5. ART and Breastfeeding Duration: Mothers with HIV should exclusively breastfeed their infants for the first six months of life, introduce appropriate complementary foods thereafter, and continue breastfeeding for the first 12 months of life. Breastfeeding should only stop once a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk can be provided. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence for the first six months and low-quality evidence for the recommendation of 12 months. 6. When to Start ART in Children: ART should be initiated in all children with HIV below five years of age, regardless of CD4 count or WHO clinical stage: Diagnosed in the first year of life (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Children aged one to below five years (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). ART should be initiated in all children aged five years and older with a CD4 count ≤500 cells/mm³, regardless of WHO clinical stage: CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). CD4 count between 350 and 500 cells/mm³ (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). ART should be initiated in all children with severe or advanced symptomatic disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4), regardless of age and CD4 count. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. ART should be initiated in any child younger than 18 months with a presumptive clinical diagnosis of HIV infection. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 7. First-Line ART Regimens: For adults and adolescents, first-line ART should consist of two nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus a non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). The preferred regimen is TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + EFV as a fixed-dose combination. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. Countries should discontinue the use of d4T in first-line regimens due to its well-recognized metabolic toxicities. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 8. Monitoring ART Response and Diagnosing Treatment Failure: Viral load testing is recommended as the preferred approach to monitor ART response and confirm treatment failure. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. If viral load testing is not routinely available, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used to diagnose treatment failure. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 9. Second-Line ART Regimens: For adults and adolescents, second-line ART should consist of two NRTIs plus a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (PI). The preferred boosted PI options are ATV/r and LPV/r. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 10. Third-Line ART Regimens: National programs should develop policies for third-line ART. Third-line regimens should include new drugs with minimal risk of cross-resistance to previously used regimens, such as integrase inhibitors and second-generation NNRTIs and PIs. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 11. Operational and Service Delivery Recommendations: Mobile phone text messages can be considered as a reminder tool to promote adherence to ART as part of a package of adherence interventions. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. In settings with a high burden of HIV and TB, ART should be initiated for individuals living with HIV in TB treatment settings, with linkage to ongoing HIV care and ART. This is a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. These recommendations are derived from the 2013 WHO guidelines on HIV care and ART use for treating and preventing HIV infection.
